children: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law prohibiting social-media platforms from showing "addictive features" to users younger than 16, part of the state's wider push to regulate what adolescents are exposed to online.

The legislation targets features common to many social-media platforms, including autoplay and technology that relies on user information to decide which content to show. It's one of 13 child-safety bills Newsom signed on Thursday, including regulations on artificial intelligence-driven chatbots and increased privacy protections.
"It's a good day for our children," Newsom said. "It's a good day for the state of California."

States have grappled for years with how to regulate social-media platforms, such as TikTok and Instagram, that have become incredibly popular among young users.  Lawmakers and lawyers have argued that some online platforms can contribute to mental-health issues, especially among adolescents, including eating disorders and self-harm.

Last month, Meta agreed to an $18 billion settlement that ended a trial over social media's impact on teenagers and required the company to make several changes to how minors interact with its platforms.

A spokesperson for Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, said delivering a tailored experience is part of what makes the platform valuable for teens. "Personalization is also how we deliver age-appropriate content for teens that is relevant to them-all with the proper guardrails in place," the spokesperson said. TikTok didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

One of the bills Newsom signed, Adam's Law, is named for Adam Raine, a 16-year-old who ended his life after having lengthy conversations with ChatGPT about suicide. That bill requires crisis protocols for suicidal ideation, parental controls, and independent child-safety audits. Another targets digitally manipulated or AI-generated material depicting minors engaging in sexual conduct.

OpenAI previously said it had implemented changes to help ChatGPT respond better to people who are in mental distress, and introduced controls that allow parents to limit the nature of conversations their children can have with the bot. A representative for the company, which publicly supported Adam's Law, said the bill "treats teens as teens when it comes to making sure AI is both safe and a tool to help contribute to their ability to learn."
